detail.what: started building kb/staging/samples.v0.json for 016 part one, and abandoned it unwritten when the other live librarian execution session committed the same file as e69238b.
detail.why_wrong: nothing about the table was wrong; the allocation was. Two librarian execution seats were live in one working copy (worktrees were reverted on 2026-09-18) and both read the same open task off tasks/. The queue is the allocation mechanism and it allocates per agent, not per session, so a second session for one agent has no way to see that a task is taken -- an open status line means open, whoever is sitting.
detail.caught_by: a message from the other session, not by a check and not by the tree. It arrived while this seat was still reading the device table for a shape to copy. Nothing on disk would have shown the collision until both files existed, and the loser would have been whichever seat committed second.
detail.outcome: backed out before writing, claimed a narrower scope by message first, and took 017's verification instead -- work the other seat explicitly could not do for itself, since it was reporting on its own commits from memory. The collision produced a better split than the queue would have: one seat writes, the other verifies.
detail.shape_to_remember: IN A SHARED WORKING COPY THE FIRST WRITE IS A RACE, AND THE QUEUE DOES NOT SETTLE IT. Claim a path by message before writing it, not after. The cost of claiming is one message; the cost of not claiming is two files, or one seat's work discarded. This is the fourth time 6.2.1's missing guard has been paid for and the first time it cost nothing, because both sessions volunteered their scope unprompted.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: nothing in the repository. Check 41 attributes a commit after the fact and check 35 refuses a boundary crossing; neither knows that two sessions share one boundary. The registry says as much in librarian-2's own note -- what a shared identity costs is attribution, what a shared path costs is refusal, and there is no refusal-level guard there since the worktrees went.

detail.what: deferred the nine data-integrity items in the prior SAFETY.md section 7, plus the mechanism behind the forbidden analogue line, and reported the deferral in a message to manager-librarian INSTEAD OF WRITING IT DOWN. The items are: PixelType reporting 12bit for 16-bit data; startSequenceAcquisition's intervalMs being ignored; ElapsedTime-ms quantised to 1 ms; MMCore raising nothing on a dropped frame; never backfilling a timestamp from host time; the host clock not being the experiment clock; relative and absolute time conventions coexisting silently; a live view degrading timing about twentyfold; and brightness failing to identify a trapped bead in a crowded field.
detail.why_wrong: the deferral was sound -- these are acquisition and clock semantics, a different slot set from 014's control paths, and they deserve their own ruling rather than being swept in on the end of one. What was wrong is where it was recorded. librarian_agent/CLAUDE.md requires dead ends in failures.jsonl precisely because an attempt abandoned without a card is recorded nowhere else, and I put it in a report. A report is context.
detail.caught_by: looking for it on 2026-09-20 in order to pick it up, and not finding it. grep across librarian_agent/ returns nothing for intervalMs, quantised timestamps or dropped frames; failures.jsonl held four records and none was this. The only reason I still knew the items existed is that a context summary carried them forward -- which is not disk, and is exactly the thing that fails on a clear.
detail.the_rule_it_broke: P1, and specifically the test CLAUDE.md names for it: clearing is how P1 gets tested, because if something vanishes when you clear it was never on disk. This would have vanished. It survived by luck, in the one form the rule says does not count.
detail.outcome: recorded here, with the nine items named, so the pickup does not depend on anyone remembering. The 10.2.1 rulings follow separately; naming the items is what makes them findable, and that is the part that was missing.
detail.shape_to_remember: a deferral REPORTED is not a deferral RECORDED. The report went to a seat above, felt like an act of disclosure, and left no trace a later session could find. I spent 2026-09-19 counting other seats for citing things they had only read in context; the same day I deferred nine items into context and called it done.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: nothing. No check reads failures.jsonl for completeness -- check 29 verifies the records that exist are well formed, which is a different question. An unwritten record and no record are the same to every check here, which is why the requirement sits in CLAUDE.md as a discipline rather than a gate.

detail.what: reported two counts about my own work from memory instead of from a run, in a session whose entire assigned output was catching exactly that. First: a verification note committed as bfa02e7 that described three items as open, when a675c4e had closed them 84 seconds earlier. Second: told manager-librarian-2 I had seven commits under the unregistered seat when `git log --committer` said six.
detail.why_wrong: librarian_agent/CLAUDE.md and the repository CLAUDE.md both say to read every count off the run and to re-read a section from disk before reporting on it. The first miss is worse than it looks: the pre-commit gate PRINTED the parent it was landing on -- `tree: the index as it would be committed, on top of a675c4e` -- and that line exists so a committer knows what tree they are on. It was printed and not read. The line is only useful to someone who treats it as a citation rather than as decoration.
detail.caught_by: the first by reading a peer's commit message minutes later; the second by running the count while writing a summary. Neither by a check. Nothing counts a seat's own commits for it and nothing rechecks a committed note against a moved tree.
detail.outcome: both corrected in the open -- the note by an appended correction in c689993 rather than an edit, the count by a follow-up message. Nothing downstream had acted on either.
detail.shape_to_remember: TWICE IN ONE SESSION, AND BOTH TIMES IN THE SAME DIRECTION: my own output counted larger than it was, and my own findings described as more open than they were. Once is a slip; the same direction twice is a bias, and the bias is flattering. The interval is the other half -- the second staleness was 84 seconds wide, not an hour, so `I only just checked` is not a defence. Re-read before reporting means before, not recently.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: for the first, reading the gate's own tree line, which is free and was already on screen. For the second, `git log --committer=<seat> | wc -l`, which is one command. Neither needs a new check; both need the run to be preferred over the memory when the memory is about my own work, which is exactly when it feels most reliable.

detail.what: told the person and two manager sessions that registering librarian-3 in contracts/seats.json would clear check 41 retroactively for the commits already made under it. It does not, and the check's own docstring says so.
detail.why_wrong: check 41 resolves each commit's committer against the registry AS IT STOOD AT THAT COMMIT'S PARENT, not against HEAD. Its docstring gives the reason: judging old commits against today's boundaries turns history red whenever a path moves between seats, and a sweep that reddens on normal activity is one nobody runs. So a registration takes effect from the next commit on, by design. I had read `check 41 reads owns, paths and excludes as data` in the registry's own growth note -- which is true and is about the check needing no code change -- and inferred from it that the check re-derives against the current file. Those are different claims and I did not open the function until the output disagreed with me.
detail.blast_radius: off a run: ten commits under this seat, eight PENDING permanently and two attributed. The eight predate 4541151 and will not clear. Nothing downstream acted on the wrong claim -- the person registered the seat anyway, which was right for other reasons -- but three readers were told a gap would close itself and it will not.
detail.caught_by: running `validate.py --commit-range` after the registration landed and seeing PENDING where I had promised clean. Not by re-reading before asserting, which is the rule this seat's CLAUDE.md states and which would have cost one grep.
detail.shape_to_remember: THIRD TIME IN ONE SESSION AND THE SAME DIRECTION ALL THREE: my own state reported better than it was. The first two, recorded in 597ab96, were counts. This one is worse and the difference is what to keep: a count is wrong about a number and a mechanism claim is wrong about what will happen, so it survives being repeated and gets acted on. It was also the cheapest to check -- one docstring, already in a file I had open for another reason that hour. WHAT MADE IT FEEL SAFE was that it was an inference from something I HAD read rather than an invention, and a true premise one step away from a false conclusion does not feel like guessing.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: reading check_41's registry lookup before saying what it does. There is a general form: when about to state what a check will do, open the check. The store already has this rule for prose and numbers -- re-read the section from disk, read every count off the run -- and it had no clause for BEHAVIOUR, which is the third thing a report can be wrong about and the only one that makes a promise.

detail.what: the blast_radius written into the previous record (432777c) understated where the retroactivity claim went. It said nothing downstream had acted on it. In fact I had written the claim into contracts/seats.json's librarian-3.registered_late field, and the person committed it in 4541151, so the false sentence is on disk in the registry that governs attribution.
detail.why_wrong: I assessed blast radius by recalling who I had TOLD, and the claim had also been WRITTEN. Those are different surfaces and only one of them survives a session. The sentence now reads `registration is retroactive, because check 41 reads this file as data and re-derives` inside the very file someone consults to find out why eight commits are PENDING -- so the next reader looking for that answer meets a sentence saying there is no problem.
detail.caught_by: the librarian manager offering to take the error as their own. Checking whether that attribution was right meant re-reading where the claim had actually gone, and the file turned up. Nobody was looking for it.
detail.shape_to_remember: A WRONG CLAIM THAT WAS ONLY SPOKEN DIES WITH THE SESSION; ONE THAT WAS FILED DOES NOT. When correcting an error, the question is not only who was told but what was written, and this seat spends its day insisting that a message is context and a file is evidence -- which cuts the same way for mistakes. It is also the reason the correction had to go to the file's owner rather than into a chat reply: the architecture seat owns seats.json, so the durable half of my own error is the half I cannot fix myself.
detail.related: 432777c records the underlying error, which stands as written; this corrects only its blast radius. Kept as a second record rather than by editing the first, for the reason rule 8 gives about entries.

detail.what: No entry was made for the refractive index of the immersion oil. Task 024 asked for three entries, one per medium; two were filed (water from Tilton and Taylor 1938, air from Meggers and Peters 1918) and oil was abandoned without one.
detail.why_wrong: Nothing about the sourcing failed -- immersion oils are well characterised and several vendors publish n_D with a temperature coefficient. What is missing is WHICH oil. The bench has no identified oil: kb/staging/samples.v0.json holds one instance, particle_suspension_a, and no oil; kb/staging/devices.v0.json has no oil row; the two oil objectives (objective_mrd71670, objective_mrd71970) name `immersion: oil` and no product. An immersion oil is not a universal constant -- Cargille Type A, Type B, LDF and Nikon's own differ in the third decimal and each moves with temperature and wavelength -- so entering a typical value would be filing a number about a bottle nobody has identified. Same shape as 015 and 017: what is missing is not the number, it is the provenance.
detail.caught_by: reading the two staging tables before searching, because task 024 said to. The search for a value was never started.
detail.outcome: A gap of kind `absent` on the SUBJECT rather than the quantity: refractive_index is now carried for water and air, and `kb_query('oil')` returns the two oil objectives and no index, so the hole is visible at the handle the caller already uses. What unblocks it is a person reading the label on the bottle, not more searching. A6 gives a number for the air and water lenses and abstains on the two oil ones, which is what 024 predicted.
detail.what_the_store_already_bounds_without_th: MRD71970's catalogue NA is 1.45 and MRD71670's is 1.42, both E3. An objective cannot have an NA above the index of its immersion medium, so the store already implies n_oil >= 1.45 without knowing the product. That is a bound and not a value, it is an inference rather than a measurement, and it was NOT entered: whether to reason from it belongs to the caller's plan, not to the store.
detail.shape_to_remember: A GAP CAN BE ABOUT THE SUBJECT RATHER THAN THE QUANTITY, and the two look identical from inside a query. `refractive_index` was never absent -- it returned eight polystyrene entries before this task and returns ten now -- while the thing A6 needed was absent the whole time. What made it findable was the class handle: putting `immersion` on the substance entries as well as the lenses means the missing one shows up as a handle that returns lenses and no medium. Compare 023, which recorded the same distinction from the other end.
detail.related: The sourcing trails that were walked and rejected for water and air are NOT here; they are in kb/sources/src_tilton_taylor_1938_water_index.json and kb/sources/src_meggers_peters_1918_air_index.json under `why_this_and_not_the_alternatives`, which is where the next person sourcing those quantities will look. Ciddor 1996 is recorded there as inaccessible, with the note that a full-text copy on a personal website was deliberately not fetched.

detail.what: edited kb/staging/devices.v0.json by loading it with json.load and writing it back with json.dump(indent=2). The change was one gap moved from `gaps` to `resolved_gaps`; the diff was 254 lines, because the file is hand-formatted with short arrays kept on one line and the dumper expanded every one of them.
detail.why_wrong: no content was altered -- the values round-tripped identically -- so no check would ever have caught it, and the commit would have passed. What it damages is a shared file: devices.v0.json is edited by more than one seat, and a 254-line reformat raises the chance of a conflict and buries the real 10-line change in noise. The repository's shared-working-copy rules are about not stepping on other seats, and a formatter is a way to step on all of them at once while changing nothing.
detail.caught_by: reading `git diff --stat` before committing and not believing the number. 254 lines for moving one object is wrong on its face. Nothing else would have said so.
detail.outcome: reverted with git checkout and redone as a text splice -- locate the object's exact source text by its unique gap_id, cut it, insert the new record after the `resolved_gaps` opening bracket, and re-parse to prove the file is still valid JSON. 24 lines. Committed as part of db2326d.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: nothing in the repository. The pre-commit gate validates the tree a commit would create and a reformat creates a valid tree. The only guard is a human reading the diff stat, which is why the number is worth looking at every time rather than only when something feels wrong.
detail.shape_to_remember: A ROUND TRIP THROUGH A FORMATTER IS AN EDIT TO EVERY LINE, and it is invisible to every check precisely because it changes nothing. The store's JSON is hand-formatted in places -- several entries keep `numbers` objects on one line -- so this is reachable from any script that loads and dumps. Before writing back, either round-trip the UNCHANGED file first and diff it against itself, which is what proved the polystyrene entries were safe to edit that way earlier today, or splice the text. The first is the cheap check and it takes one line.
detail.related: the polystyrene degC-to-kelvin edit under 024 used the same json.dump route and was safe, because that file was already in indent=2 form -- verified by a self-round-trip before touching it. Doing the check there and skipping it here is the whole of the difference.

detail.what: Re-derived task 029's three camera transfers from agentic-microscope -- opened data/detectors.yaml, read the per-mode table, the QE-curve borrow note and the sensor geometry -- before finding the eight entries already filed and committed at db2326d.
detail.why_wrong: Nothing about the derivation was wrong. detail.outcome: Abandoned before any write. No entry, no edit, no duplicate, and no kb_query call -- the reading was of the prior repository's files, which section 10.2 row 3 has open. The only cost was one read pass.
detail.shape_to_remember: A TASK'S STATUS LINE IS PROSE. The root CLAUDE.md says to read counts off a run and never off prose, and names three counts that were wrong within a day in both directions. That sentence covers the queue's own open/closed field too, and nothing anywhere says so -- the single instruction this seat is given for picking up work points it at precisely the kind of field that rule distrusts. The run that replaces it: ask what artefact the task produces and run `git log -1 -- <that path>`. Empty means not done; a commit means done, whatever the header says.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: nothing in the repository. No check compares a task's status line against the tree -- check 29 validates the shape of failure records and nothing validates the shape or the truth of a task header. The guard is the seat naming the artefact before starting.

detail.what: Edited tracer_diffusivity_expected by loading it with json.load and writing it back with json.dump(indent=4). The change was one sentence inside one string; the diff was 21 added and 21 removed on a 23-line file, because the file is indent 2 and the dumper wrote 4.
detail.why_wrong: Identical in shape to the 029 record already in this file: a round trip through a formatter is an edit to every line. Content round-tripped unchanged, so no check would have caught it and the commit would have passed. What it damages is a shared tree -- a whole-file rewrite raises the chance of a conflict with the OTHER librarian execution seat working in this same directory today, and buries a one-line change in noise.
detail.caught_by: reading `git diff --numstat` before committing. 21 added and 21 removed for one sentence is wrong on its face.
detail.outcome: Reverted with git checkout, redone as a raw text splice on the file's bytes with a json.loads() before writing to prove it still parses. 1 added, 1 removed. Committed as c708120.
detail.what_this_adds_over_the_029_record: THE RECORD DID NOT PREVENT IT. This seat read the 029 entry -- the one that names this exact shape in capitals -- a few hours before walking into it, in this same session, while surveying failures.jsonl. So the guard is not having the record and it is not having read the record; the guard is looking at the diff stat on every write. That is what the 029 record itself says, and this is the evidence that it means it literally. A second instance is also what tells the two apart: one occurrence is a seat being careless, two with a read record in between is a procedure that only works at the point of the number.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: nothing in the repository, same as 029. The pre-commit gate validates the tree a commit would create and a reformat creates a valid tree.

detail.what: Edited librarian_agent/src/mcp_server.py's kb_query projection -- adding `kind` and `valid_until` -- while the OTHER live librarian execution seat was editing the same function for the same task. Backed out my whole 43-line insertion and left their 82 lines untouched. Net effect on the tree: nothing.
detail.why_wrong: I never claimed the path. seats.json's librarian-3 `unguarded` field records what actually held on 2026-09-19 when two librarian seats shared this directory: they claimed paths by message BEFORE writing, one wrote while the other verified, and it cost one abandoned table. That is a practice and not a guard -- nothing refuses a second writer -- so skipping the message is the whole of the failure. I read the projection, spent six tool calls measuring, and wrote; their edit landed inside that window.
detail.caught_by: reading back the lines I had just written with `sed -n` and not recognising them. The text at the line numbers I had patched was about `symbol` being null on 103 entries, which I had not written. Then `git status`, which showed mcp_server.py modified where it had been clean at session start and showed validate.py, failures.jsonl and queries/log.jsonl newly COMMITTED -- the other seat had committed three files and opened a fourth in the time I was measuring.
detail.what_my_own_precheck_would_not_have_caug: My splice asserted the anchor text occurred exactly once and it did, because their edit inserted ABOVE the anchor and left it intact. A uniqueness check on the anchor is not a check that the file is the one you read. The root CLAUDE.md's rule -- run `git diff -- <paths>` first and check every hunk is yours -- is aimed at commit time, and this was a WRITE-time collision: at the moment I wrote there was no diff of mine to inspect yet, and a clean `git status` taken six calls earlier was already stale.

detail.why_wrong: A DECISION TAKES NO GRADE. plan.md:1259 @6d587b3: `A policy takes no grade -- because it is a decision, not a claim. P2's four parts (value, unit, source, grade) attach to A CLAIM ABOUT THE WORLD.` Not repeating a calibration is not a claim about the world. And kb_entry.schema.json REQUIRES `grade`, so there is no way to file a decision in kb/entries/ without giving it the one thing it must not have -- the withdrawal is forced by the schema rather than chosen.
detail.the_right_reading_was_in_my_own_instruct: librarian_agent/CLAUDE.md says plainly that `we do not exceed Y` is policy, belongs to a person, and is not knowledge. I read it, weighed it against this exact entry, and TALKED MYSELF OUT OF IT on the ground that the sentence sits beside `envelope/safety.*` and so must be about safety limits. The safety ceiling is the INSTANCE; plan.md states the principle generally. I reasoned about the sentence's neighbourhood instead of reading what it said.
detail.and_i_flagged_it_while_getting_it_wrong: The entry itself and the source record both said IN CAPITALS that the fit was a seam -- that this half is an intent rather than a judgement and that the store has no kind for it. So the defect was visible to me at the moment of writing and I filed it anyway, with a paragraph explaining why the misfit was tolerable. A FLAG IS NOT A FIX, AND A WELL-WRITTEN FLAG IS THE MOST CONVINCING FORM OF THE ERROR: the note made the entry read as considered rather than as wrong, which is exactly what stops a reviewer looking again. WHEN AN ENTRY NEEDS A PARAGRAPH EXPLAINING WHY IT ALMOST FITS, IT DOES NOT FIT.
detail.caught_by: manager-simulation, from the other side, reading the published snapshot. It asked whether the two halves of one ruling really belonged under one `assumed:`, and named 5.3.1's targets -- `assumed:a_target` E5 ceasing to be how a person's target is recorded -- as the precedent.

detail.a_second_smaller_deviation_inside_this_o: The first attempt to write THIS record never reached disk. It was the tail of a `cmd && cmd && python3 - <<PY` chain whose first link was export_snapshot.py, which correctly refused to publish from an uncommitted store -- so the chain short-circuited and the append silently did not happen, while the commit that followed named failures.jsonl and committed four files without it. Caught by grepping the file for the record rather than trusting that the heredoc had run. AN && CHAIN MAKES A WRITE CONDITIONAL ON AN UNRELATED COMMAND SUCCEEDING, and the failure is silent because the shell reports the first command's exit and not the last one's absence.
detail.shape_to_remember: A PUBLISHED VERSION KEEPS THE ERROR AND THAT IS THE DESIGN WORKING. kbv-a8817e71e17b contains the withdrawn entry and always will; a consumer pinned there holds a store that is internally consistent and simply wrong about one thing, and the fix is a later version rather than a rewrite -- the same argument the rename ruling made on 2026-09-20. The cost of publishing a mistake is therefore bounded, and the cost of not publishing until certain is not.

detail.what: ran the three pre-commit checks on 655 log lines and committed 657. Two lines arrived between the check and the commit and went into 67860f2 without being inspected. They were benign -- two more absent queries from the same question -- and that is luck, not procedure.
detail.why_wrong: `git commit -- <path>` builds its index from the WORKTREE state of that path at commit time, not from the state that was checked. The repository's CLAUDE.md says this about other seats' edits and says the window measured three minutes once; the same window exists on a file only this seat writes, because the writer is not a seat at all -- it is five MCP servers appending whenever any agent calls the store. Naming a path is not naming a change, and that holds when the other writer is a process.
detail.caught_by: re-running the strict-prefix check on the NEXT notification and finding HEAD already at 657 when the last inspected count was 655. Not by any check -- the gate validates the tree a commit creates and an append-only log creates a valid tree either way.
detail.outcome: no damage: the strict-prefix check verified bytes 1..655 are unchanged, and a later run verified 1..657 against the new HEAD, so nothing was rewritten in the window. The two uninspected lines are readable now and are what they appeared to be.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: re-running the prefix check AFTER the commit against the new HEAD, which costs one command. The check before the commit answers 'is what I am about to commit an append?' and the check after answers 'is what I did commit one?' -- and only the second is about the bytes that actually landed.
detail.shape_to_remember: A CHECK BEFORE A COMMIT DESCRIBES A TREE THAT MAY NOT BE THE ONE COMMITTED, and for this file the other writer is not a colleague who can be messaged -- it is a server that appends on somebody else's call. The three checks are still worth running before, because refusing to commit is only possible before; but the claim 'this commit is a pure append' is only established after. This seat wrote 'strict append at 655 lines' into commit messages that carried 657.
detail.related: same family as the 029 formatter near-miss in this file: a content-preserving operation that no check can see. There the guard was reading the diff stat; here it is re-reading the prefix after the fact.

detail.what: wrote into two commit messages (49e9d8d, bf5942b) that the engine-cost absents were a NEW PATTERN appearing across two commits, naming cost_per_particle_step_yukawa_2d and cost_per_particle_step_overdamped. Counted afterwards over the whole log: the same question had already been asked four times as particle_step_rate, by sim-20260923-041 and -042 across both their configurations. Six asks, three names, and every one of the six on axis a5. The pattern was real and older than I said, and I had called two renamings of it new.
detail.why_wrong: I read the pattern off the four lines in front of me instead of counting the 750 behind them. Two new-looking names in consecutive commits look like an emerging trend precisely because the prior asks used a different name -- which is the thing worth reporting, and I missed it by not looking. The repository's own CLAUDE.md says READ EVERY COUNT OFF THE RUN, NEVER OFF PROSE and names three counts that were wrong within a day; this is the same defect one level down, reading a TREND off a window instead of a run. Filed as `deviation`: the six kinds come from plan.md 8.1 and I invented a seventh, `wrong_claim`, by reading the kinds off the neighbouring rows instead of off the enum -- the same defect as the entry itself, one level down again. Check 29 refused the commit and named it, which is the gate doing exactly what the rest of this file says no check can do for the hazards that have none.
detail.caught_by: running the count I should have run first, to decide whether the claim was worth reporting up. The count contradicted the claim I had already committed.
detail.outcome: no knowledge was corrupted -- nothing entered the KB and no entry cites any of this. The cost is two commit messages in the permanent record that overstate what they saw, corrected in the next message rather than amended, because --amend is forbidden in this working copy. The corrected numbers (450 kb_query calls with a caller_id, 138 distinct observables, 38 that ever returned anything, 100 never answered) went to the simulation design seat, who ruled one name with the engine in validity_conditions.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: the count, before the claim. It cost one script and forty seconds. The asymmetry is the lesson: the count was cheap enough that there was no reason to guess, and I guessed because a commit message felt like a place for an impression rather than a measurement.
detail.shape_to_remember: A GAP COUNTED OVER A WINDOW IS NOT A PATTERN, AND RENAMING HIDES AGE. When a name looks new, search the log for the QUANTITY and not the NAME -- two of these three names had the engine baked in, so no string search on either would have found the other four asks. The same reflex that makes a count trustworthy (run it, do not read it) applies to the claim that something is new: novelty is a count over history, not an observation about the last few lines.
detail.related: the immediately useful half of the corrected count was not the absence but the NAMING -- an observable with the system baked into its name can only ever be answered for that system, which is entry rule 2's boundary seen from the caller's side. That half only appeared because the count forced me to look at all three names together.

detail.what: committed into the message of the log commit at 761 lines that the store HOLDS the disk period and that a caller asking `disk_period` was being told absent because the quantity name did not reach the entry -- 'not missing knowledge, unreachable knowledge', and that eight absent gaps in other agents' cards were therefore wrong. Then opened the entry. csuw1_disk_speed_exposure_constraint carries `numbers: null`. It states a CONSTRAINT -- an exposure must last an integer multiple of the disk period -- and never says what the period is. No entry anywhere in the store carries a number with `period` in its name. The eight absent answers were correct.
detail.why_wrong: I inferred what an entry contains from the fact that it ANSWERED a query, and from a sentence about it quoted in check 72's output. Answering means the subject matched, not that a number is inside. My whole basis for the strongest claim in that message was a coverage word and a quoted clause, neither of which is the entry.
detail.caught_by: opening the entry before reporting the finding to other seats. The count that produced the finding was right -- disk_period 8 asks absent, csuw1_disk_speed_exposure_constraint 7 asks answered -- and the interpretation laid over it was wrong.
detail.outcome: the false claim is in the commit message at 761 lines and is corrected in the message of this commit, not amended. Nothing was sent to another seat and no entry was edited, because the check happened before either. What survives is milder and real: the store serves a constraint 7 times whose operand it does not hold, so a caller who receives it cannot apply it without the separately-absent disk_period. That is a design observation about relation entries, not unreachable knowledge.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: one `json.load` of the entry, before writing the claim. Same cost as the count that preceded it.
detail.shape_to_remember: THIS IS THE THIRD TIME IN ONE SESSION AND THE REPETITION IS THE FINDING. First: called the engine-cost absents a new pattern, read off four log lines instead of counted. Second: invented failure kind `wrong_claim`, read off the neighbouring rows instead of the enum. Third: said the store holds the disk period, read off a coverage word instead of the entry. One shape -- I AM ACCURATE ABOUT THE QUERY LOG AND CARELESS ABOUT EVERYTHING ELSE I CITE, because the log is the artifact I am watching and the rest feels like background I already know. The log being counted honestly is what makes the wrong layer on top of it sound authoritative. So: BEFORE ANY CLAIM ABOUT WHAT THE STORE HOLDS, OPEN THE ENTRY -- the count is evidence about questions, never about contents.
detail.related: the enum instance is the same defect with a check to catch it and this one has none, which is the split the root CLAUDE.md keeps drawing. Check 29 refused the invented kind in seconds; nothing at all would have stopped the disk_period claim from reaching another seat as a fact about my own store.

detail.what: to test whether CRLF checkout was why kb_index --check called a clean tree stale, hashed a `git archive HEAD` extraction as the 'committed bytes' control. It gave kbv-2b3ce8932bde, the same as the checkout, which read as 'line endings are not the cause'.

detail.outcome: fix landed in 39a1c75; nothing wrong was written or sent
detail.shape_to_remember: on a Windows checkout, the only unconverted view of committed content is the object store: `git cat-file blob` or `git show <rev>:<path>`. archive and checkout both convert.
